To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
defect-free thin polyimide layers can be deposited on alumina supports using polymer solutions with viscosities higher than the entanglement viscosity.
the viscosity of the polyimide solution plays a major role in the formation of defect-free ceramic-supported thin polyamide films.

the entanglement concentrations of the polymers studied were 3.1 wt. % for 6FDA- 6FpDA and 3.52 % for Matrimide®; the entanglement value for P84® could not be determined due to the high viscosity of the solutions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the production of thin polyimide layers with good adhesion on ceramic supports for high temperature gas separation applications.
the fabrication of thin polyimide membranes on porous alumina supports for gas separation applications at high temperature.
the fabrication of ceramic-supported thin polymeric films for gas separation applications at elevated temperatures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed ceramic-supported polyimide thin films can be considered as a novel class of membranes for gas separation applications at elevated temperatures.
the best polymer for gas separation at elevated temperatures is 6FDA- 6FpDA.
a high H2/CO selectivity can be obtained at elevated temperatures with the 6FDA-based polymer, while a high H2/N2 selectivity is achieved by using Matrimid®.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the polyimide 6FDA- 6FpDA shows the highest selectivities at high temperatures and is the best choice for the fabrication of ceramic-supported thin films for high temperature membrane applications.
the best membrane performance for gas separation is achieved with the thinnest film possible, and the best temperature for gas separation is the highest possible.
the use of ceramic supports for thin polyimide membranes is a viable option for high-temperature gas separations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of a polymer solution with a concentration below the C* value leads to defect-free films with a higher permeance and a lower selectivity than films prepared with a polymer solution with concentration above the C* value.
the use of ceramic-supported thin polymeric films can provide a viable option for gas separations at high temperatures.
the entanglement of polymer chains plays a major role in determining the properties of the resulting thin film.
